title: The Art of Being Present
author: The Mindful Manager
summary: The Mindful Manager builds on an earlier piece about switching off from work to address the harder problem: not just leaving work behind physically, but fully arriving wherever you actually are — whether that's a family holiday, a conversation with a colleague, or a meeting. The core argument is that presence is a practice, not a fixed trait, requiring only the willingness to notice when attention has wandered and gently return it, 'again, and again, and again,' rather than achieving some perfected empty-mind state. The piece introduces 'somatic intelligence' as a second route back to presence: since the mind often drifts before we consciously notice, physical signals like tight shoulders, a clenched jaw, or a dropping stomach can serve as early clues that attention has left the present moment, functioning as information to investigate rather than sensations to suppress. The author explicitly ties this personal practice back to professional performance, arguing that presence rehearsed in ordinary moments — listening to a child's long story, sharing a meal — transfers directly into the workplace, where it improves listening, noticing, and connection, closing on the claim that 'the greatest gift we can give someone... is our full attention.'
points: The reframe of presence as 'a practice' rather than a trait — 'presence isn't perfection, it's returning' — lowers the bar for readers who assume mindfulness requires eliminating distraction rather than simply noticing and redirecting it repeatedly.

Somatic intelligence gives a concrete, actionable diagnostic: physical signals (tight shoulders, a clenched jaw, a dropping stomach before opening an inbox) function as early-warning clues that attention has left the present moment, even before the mind consciously registers it.

The explicit transfer claim — that presence rehearsed in ordinary family moments carries directly into workplace performance (listening more carefully, noticing more, connecting better) — gives leaders a professional rationale for practicing presence outside of work, not just a wellness one.

The three concrete techniques offered (slow deep breaths, attention to physical senses, letting thoughts come and go without engaging them) are simple enough to apply in real time during a stressful meeting, not just on holiday.
quotes: It's entirely possible to be sitting beside a swimming pool while mentally rehearsing next week's presentation. To be building sandcastles with your children while replying to emails in your head.
Being present is about giving your brain permission to experience what's actually happening instead of constantly predicting, planning or problem solving.

You don't need to meditate for an hour every morning or empty your mind. You simply need to notice when your attention has wandered and gently bring it back. Again. And again. And again. Presence isn't perfection. It's returning.
Somatic intelligence is our ability to notice the physical sensations that accompany our thoughts and emotions, and use them as information rather than ignoring them.
Maybe your stomach drops before opening your inbox, even when you're technically on holiday. Those sensations can be clues.

The more we practise being present while playing with our children, sharing a meal with friends or walking the dog, the easier it becomes to bring that same presence into the workplace. We listen more carefully. We notice more. We connect better.
The greatest gift we can give someone isn't always our advice or our expertise, sometimes it's our full attention.
